titulo.texto: Traditional Red Triqui huipil from San Juan Copala

frase_gancho.texto: An intense red woven in three panels, with butterflies and suns.

puente_narrativo.texto: From textile we move on to clay. Look for vessels in a shiny black, with openwork in the shape of flowers, that look like polished metal.

guion_corto.texto: This long, intensely red huipil belongs to Triqui women, a people of the Mixtec region of Oaxaca. It is woven on a backstrap loom, in three joined panels, and decorated with horizontal bands of brocade: figures of butterflies, suns, stars and furrows of the milpa. Notice the density of the weave and the colorful tassels hanging down the back. The cotton threads are dyed red with dyes that used to come mostly from cochineal. For Triqui women, this huipil identifies their people anywhere. Today many families migrate for work or because of violence, and they carry their huipil with them as a way of continuing to be Triqui, wherever they may be.

guion_largo.texto:
If anything identifies a Triqui woman, it is her red huipil. That red is so strong that it can be recognized from far away, in a plaza or on a city street. It is not a garment meant to go unnoticed. It is a declaration of belonging, woven with thread.

The Triqui are a small people of the Mixtec region of Oaxaca, with their own language, which belongs to the same great family as Mixtec. They live in a mountainous region, close to some of the places where the cochineal was raised. That is why the red of their huipiles is associated with that dye, although today industrial dyes are also used.

Notice the shape. There are three panels, woven on a backstrap loom and joined at the edges, as in the entrance huipil you saw on the Upper Floor. The Triqui huipil is long, sometimes down to the ankles. Nothing is cut from the cloth: the shape depends on the width of the loom, and the design on the talent of the weaver.

Then comes the brocade. These are the horizontal bands you see, made with an extra thread that is worked into the weft while weaving. The designs include butterflies, suns, stars and furrows of the milpa, as well as broken lines. These geometric bands recall, in their spirit, the [stone fretwork of Mitla](mna_s07_grecas_mitla) that you saw in the Oaxaca Hall downstairs. It is as if the same taste for order and rhythm had passed from stone to cloth.

The butterflies deserve a pause. They are a frequent animal in textile tradition and in the imagination of many peoples. They are associated with the soul and with transformation, and you already saw a butterfly on the chest of the [Atlas figure of Tula](mna_s05_atlante_tula). Here they appear on the huipiles, and whoever wears them takes on a symbol of life and change.

Triqui is, moreover, a tonal language: the meaning of a word changes according to the tone with which it is pronounced, as in Chinese. A huipil like this can take months to weave, and each woman usually weaves several over her lifetime: the everyday one, the festive one and, according to some families, the most carefully made, which will accompany her to the end.

The recent history of the Triqui has been difficult. Their region has experienced conflict and poverty, and many families have had to leave their villages. Today there are Triqui communities in Mexico City and in other states in the north of the country. Many women keep the huipil, and they do so with pride. It is a way of saying: “my people are still here, wherever we may be.”

This garment shows it: a huipil is not just clothing, it is memory that travels. It can be woven in a mountain range of Oaxaca, worn in a market in the capital and passed from mother to daughter. In each of those steps, the red remains the red of its people.

texto: Look for the brocade bands with butterflies and suns
Count the three panels that make up the huipil
Notice the colorful tassels hanging down the back

texto.Region: San Juan Copala, Mixteca Baja, Oaxaca
texto.Technique/Material: Cotton woven on a backstrap loom with supplementary-weft brocade and ribbons
texto.Function: Everyday and ceremonial clothing of high rank and community identity

texto.pregunta: Myth: The red huipiles of Oaxaca are all made the same way, everywhere.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Each people has its own designs and its own red. The Triqui huipil is recognized by its three panels, its geometric brocade and its tassels.
